intro: Every sport leaves paper behind. Clubs write constitutions. Committees vote on rules and print them in yearly editions. Leagues keep minutes of their meetings. Fans save scorebooks, tickets and programs. Architects draw plans for fields and stands. Each of these papers carries a date and the name of the person or body that made it.

In this unit, you pick up one sport's papers and read them as a historian does. You will follow the Football Association from its 1863 meeting in London, the National League from its 1876 constitution, and college football from the crisis of 1905. You will read the 1867 baseball report that shut out Black clubs and the 1921 resolution that closed English grounds to women's teams. Then you will visit the halls and archives that keep sport's objects, from Cooperstown in 1939 to Kansas City in 1990.

By the end, you will be able to name the body behind a rule, date it, and say who it let in or kept out. You will be able to tell a record made at the time from a legend told later. You will also be able to write a clear caption for a sports object: what it is, who made it, when, and how it reached the collection.
bigQuestion: What can one sport's papers and objects prove about who held power in it, and who was written out?

timeline.t: The Knickerbocker Base Ball Club of New York writes down twenty rules
The Football Association forms in London and adopts thirteen Laws of the Game
A national baseball committee recommends barring clubs with Black members
Eight clubs adopt the National League constitution in New York
The International Football Association Board first meets in London
The Triangle prints Naismith's thirteen basketball rules
Sixty-two colleges found the IAAUS, later renamed the NCAA
Rube Foster and other owners found the Negro National League in Kansas City
The FA bars women's teams from its members' grounds
The National Baseball Hall of Fame is dedicated in Cooperstown
The Negro Leagues Baseball Museum is founded in Kansas City
Major League Baseball recognizes seven Negro Leagues as major leagues

words.d: the founding document of a body; it says who may join, who leads and how decisions are made
the written rules of a game, usually issued in yearly editions
an organization with the power to set rules and run competitions for a sport
the rules that decide who may take part in a sport
a rule or practice that kept Black people out of teams, leagues or places
a formal decision voted on and recorded by a body
a record made at the time by people who were there
a traditional story told as history that records do not support
a short note naming the body, document and year a fact came from
the record of who owned an object and when
a collection of papers, photographs and records kept mainly for study
a short museum label saying what an object is, who made it, when and where, and how it was acquired

test.q: In what year did the Football Association adopt its first Laws of the Game?
test.why: The FA adopted thirteen Laws on 8 December 1863.

test.q: Which paper would tell you who could vote in the 1876 National League?
test.why: A constitution sets out a body's members and how they vote.

test.q: Which body has changed soccer's Laws since 1886?
test.why: Only the IFAB, which first met in 1886, can change the Laws.

choices: The Baseball Hall of Fame opened.
test.why: The IAAUS, renamed the NCAA in 1910, was founded on that date.

test.q: Which city hosted the 1920 meeting that began the national federation of high school associations?
test.why: L. W. Smith of the Illinois association hosted the meeting in Chicago on 14 May 1920.

test.q: Why is the December 1867 report important evidence?
choices: It put baseball's exclusion of Black clubs in writing.
test.why: The committee's report is a written record of exclusion by a national body.

test.q: How did the major league color line mostly work from the late 1880s to 1947?
choices: by a printed rule in the league constitution
by an unwritten agreement among owners
by a vote of the players
test.why: No major league printed a ban; owners simply did not sign Black players.

test.q: Who founded the Negro National League in 1920?
test.why: Rube Foster of the Chicago American Giants led the founding meeting in Kansas City.

test.q: What did the FA's 1921 resolution close to women's teams?
choices: the grounds of FA member clubs
test.why: The resolution asked member clubs not to let women's teams use their grounds.

test.q: Why do historians call the Doubleday story a legend?
choices: The records do not support it, and Doubleday was at West Point in 1839.
Doubleday wrote a memoir denying it.
test.why: The claim rested on one man's childhood memory, and Doubleday never claimed it.

test.q: Who helped create the baseball box score around 1859?
test.why: Henry Chadwick adapted cricket scoring into the box score.

choices: the date a rule was written
the record of who owned an object and when
the body that wrote a rule
test.why: Provenance traces an object's owners from its maker to today.

choices: the National Baseball Hall of Fame
the Pro Football Hall of Fame
test.why: The Baseball Hall of Fame was dedicated in 1939, before the others.

test.q: What did Major League Baseball announce on 16 December 2020?
choices: It would count seven Negro Leagues as major leagues.
It would move the Hall of Fame.
It would drop the box score.
test.why: MLB recognized seven Negro Leagues from 1920 to 1948 as major leagues.

test.q: Which caption is written from the record?
choices: The oldest ball in the world.
Homemade baseball, 1800s, found in Fly Creek, New York, in 1934.
test.why: A good caption says what the object is and where it came from, without claiming a legend.

write.prompt: Pick one sport from this unit. Using at least three of its dated papers or objects, such as a constitution, a rule book, a resolution or a museum record, explain who wrote the sport's rules, who was written in or out, and when that changed.
tips: Cite each paper by body, title and year, such as Football Association, council resolution, 1921.
Say which body held power: a club, a league, a committee or a school association.
Separate records made at the time from stories told later, and label legends as legends.
Use unit words like color line, eligibility, provenance and primary source.
Tell what changed and when, and compare before and after instead of judging people.
